title: Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a widely usable digital payment instrument that combines meaningful privacy in everyday transactions with reliable payment integrity, operation during connectivity failures, loss recovery and legally governed safeguards. Users would be able to pay without routinely exposing sensitive payment information to parties that do not need it, while the system maintains valid payments and clearly defined responsibilities. The combined capability remains a design goal; the supplied evidence demonstrates an exploratory foundation.

Conceptual synthesis: the central challenge is making these properties work together. Offline payments must preserve payment integrity when participants cannot immediately consult a shared record. Recovery must help legitimate owners without creating an easy route to duplicate claims or unauthorized access. Legal controls must specify who may obtain information, under what authority and with what accountability. These are additional requirements of this concept, not capabilities established by the supplied Aurum evidence.

significance.text: Achieving this combination could extend important properties of physical cash into digital commerce: everyday payment privacy and the ability to transact during connectivity failures. The Aurum project supplies a foundation for the privacy component by exploring how payment integrity and regulatory safeguards can coexist with restricted visibility of sensitive payment information. It does not establish the full proposed combination.

Conditional implications: reliable offline operation could let people continue essential transactions during outages and make digital payments more useful where connectivity is intermittent. Strong privacy protections could reduce routine exposure of payment histories. Accessible devices and usable recovery procedures could broaden participation, but those benefits would depend on affordability, merchant acceptance, operational reliability and the actual experience of people with limited technical resources. Adoption does not follow automatically from technical feasibility.

Limits of the cash analogy: protection against theft and unauthorized surveillance would require demonstrated security and effective institutional enforcement. Cash-like privacy does not by itself imply absolute anonymity, and resilient digital money would still depend on devices, power and operating rules. Recovery and legally authorized investigation introduce questions about access and control that the analogy to physical cash cannot resolve.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a convincingly demonstrated system that achieves the proposed privacy, integrity, resilience, recovery and legal safeguards together within explicit operating limits. Aurum documents the challenge of balancing privacy, integrity and regulatory requirements, including possible trade-offs involving programmability, performance and operational complexity. The supplied project page does not establish how far those trade-offs can be reduced at deployment scale or whether the complete concept remains unsolved across the field.

Engineering questions for the broader concept include how to prevent or bound double-spending during repeated offline transfers, how to recognize compromised devices, and how to reconcile transactions after connectivity returns. An offline recipient needs a defensible basis for accepting value without immediate access to an authoritative shared record. The supplied review does not establish Aurum's mechanisms or results for these questions; they remain requirements to investigate rather than findings about its implementation.

Recovery and investigation create further design questions. A system must distinguish legitimate recovery from fraudulent attempts to reclaim already transferred funds, define what happens when a device or credential is lost, and determine what information any investigator or recovery operator can access. Proposed safeguards need technical enforcement, authorization rules and auditable institutional processes. Technology can implement a chosen allocation of powers, but choosing those powers also requires law and policy.

current_state.text: Project Aurum Phase 2 produced an exploratory proof of concept for privacy-preserving digital cash. According to the supplied review of the BIS Innovation Hub landing page, it combines privacy technologies with payment-integrity and compliance mechanisms, separates responsibilities and data access, and provides a practical reference that policymakers can adapt to their objectives and regulatory requirements. This supports the feasibility of an architectural component and further experimentation, rather than establishing a production-ready payment system.

The page reports an update and associated publication dated 13 October 2026. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate mass deployment, robust repeated offline circulation, loss recovery, resistance to device compromise or resolution of governance trade-offs. Those limits describe what this evidence establishes; they do not prove that such capabilities are absent from Aurum's wider work or from other projects. No quantitative performance, deployment-scale or failure-rate result is established in the supplied review.

Evidence access is limited to the project landing page as assessed in the supplied review. Its saved extraction was not truncated and recorded no extraction issues, but the linked technical report and detailed validation were not supplied. Consequently, the evidence is partial for evaluating the project as a whole. The 13 October date precedes the review's 1 November 2026 cutoff, while the saved page was retrieved on 11 November 2026; that later retrieval does not independently establish the page's exact contents at the cutoff. The supplied research record also does not provide broader coverage of competing or subsequent work.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a legally grounded system at substantial scale, with the participant and merchant population, transaction volume, outage duration, offline-transfer depth and acceptable failure rates specified before evaluation. Trials should include repeated offline transfers, realistic outages and reconnection, with explicit tests of payment integrity and treatment of conflicting transactions. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not established standards or requirements prescribed by Aurum.
completion_criteria.label: Legally grounded payments demonstrate integrity at scale through offline transfers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed independent assessment: determine what each participant, intermediary, operator and authorized authority can learn from normal payments and exceptional procedures. Test device loss, device compromise, fraudulent recovery attempts and the information exposed during recovery or investigation. Evaluate exceptional-access authorization, enforcement and audit, including attempts to exceed an actor's permitted powers. Privacy claims should identify the actors and circumstances against which protection is demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Independent assessment tests actor-specific privacy and exceptional-access safeguards

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the architecture, threat assumptions, evaluation methods and sufficiently detailed results available for independent scrutiny and replication. Assess usability and affordability for people with limited connectivity or technical resources, and report dependence on devices, power, transaction limits and maximum offline duration. Repeated evaluations should show whether the claimed properties survive realistic operational conditions. Finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality or immunity to every future attack.
completion_criteria.label: Replicable evaluations report practical limits under realistic operational conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: FIN-06, universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer, has the closest overlap because both concern usable payment infrastructure. FIN-06 emphasizes reach and transfer speed across jurisdictions; FIN-07 emphasizes privacy, resilience and safeguards during everyday use. A payment instrument could contribute to both, but success on either set of requirements would not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-02, causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades, and FIN-03, run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment, share a concern with financial resilience. FIN-07 addresses continuity and integrity of payments during operational disruption. It does not itself solve contagion forecasting or the financing mismatch between liquid claims and illiquid investment. FIN-08, a causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes, likewise concerns a distinct market mechanism rather than offline payment integrity.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-04, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods, and FIN-05, financing without conventional credit histories, could benefit from accessible payment infrastructure, but still require their own advances in insurance and credit provision. FIN-10, financing mechanisms for pure public goods, could use such infrastructure to move funds, yet its central challenge is generating and coordinating funding rather than protecting individual transactions.

Roster-based synthesis: FIN-11, operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage, has a limited connection through information availability, but its focus is financial value and arbitrage rather than privacy rights or payment authorization. FIN-01, a general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior, and FIN-09, causal measurement of investment's financial and real-world impact, address explanatory and measurement problems. Their relationship to FIN-07 is indirect; they remain distinct innovations.

change_log.reason: The research and review support retaining the innovation, while distinguishing its intended combined capability from the exploratory component demonstrated.

change_log.change: Separated the documented privacy–integrity–compliance challenge from proposed offline, compromise, recovery and investigative-access requirements.
change_log.reason: The supplied source does not substantiate those additional mechanisms in sufficient detail; their evidentiary limits do not justify deleting the requirements.

change_log.change: Made the consequences conditional and clarified the limits of the physical-cash analogy.
change_log.reason: Offline resilience, theft resistance, institutional enforcement and adoption require additional demonstrations beyond privacy-preserving architecture.

change_log.change: Integrated Aurum's architectural contribution, exploratory scope, dated publication information and access limitations.
change_log.reason: The landing page supports a proof of concept, while the missing technical report limits assessment of performance, deployment and detailed validation.

change_log.change: Added explicit payment-integrity testing, predefined operating thresholds, reproducibility and practical boundaries to the proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: These make the demonstration assessable without presenting proposed thresholds as consensus standards or finite testing as universal proof.

change_log.change: Added differentiated relationships to the supplied concept roster.
change_log.reason: Payment infrastructure, financial resilience, inclusion and information have relevant connections, but the entries address distinct capabilities and remain separate.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish Aurum's offline-transfer, recovery or device-compromise mechanisms or their measured performance.
The linked technical report and detailed validation were not supplied, so the landing-page assessment cannot resolve implementation or deployment questions.
The evidence does not establish the present field-wide availability or absence of the full combined capability, nor comprehensive coverage of competing or subsequent work.
The exact contents of the project page at the 1 November 2026 cutoff are not independently established by its 11 November retrieval.
Substantial scale, acceptable failure rates, maximum outage duration and offline-transfer depth remain to be specified for a concrete completion decision.
The acceptable balance among privacy, recovery, investigative access and institutional authority remains a legal and policy question as well as an engineering requirement.

brief.title: Private digital money that works without internet
possible: You could pay during an internet outage without routinely sharing sensitive payment details with parties that do not need them. Money received without a connection could be spent again. Lost funds could be recovered, while safeguards kept payments valid and governed access for investigations.
why: People and shops could keep essential transactions going during outages and in places with unreliable connections. Less routine exposure of spending histories would bring an important protection of physical cash into digital commerce.

sources.who: BIS Innovation Hub Hong Kong Centre and collaborators
sources.showed: Project Aurum built an exploratory digital cash prototype that combines payment privacy with regulatory controls. Its design separates responsibilities and access to payment information.
sources.quote: It illustrates how responsibilities and data access can be separated across the system, while preserving payment integrity.
sources.cited_for: It supports building privacy protections into payment systems alongside controls that keep payments valid.
sources.not_established: The prototype does not establish reliable offline circulation, loss recovery or operation at broad scale.

sources.who: Carolin Beer, Sheila Zingg, Kari Kostiainen and collaborators
sources.showed: PayOff combines anonymous payments without a connection with limits on wallet balances. It lets the central bank identify creators and recipients of counterfeit money when protected hardware is compromised.
sources.quote: Our evaluation shows that offline payments are fast and that the central bank can handle high payment loads using moderate computing resources.
sources.cited_for: It supports combining private offline payments with targeted identification of counterfeit money flows.
sources.not_established: It does not establish the full combination with loss recovery and independently assessed limits on investigative access.

sources.who: Panagiotis Michalopoulos, Anthony Mack, Cameron Clark and collaborators
sources.showed: A preprint reports an offline payment prototype using smart cards with protected chips to enforce payment rules. Stronger privacy through mathematical proofs remains conceptual.
sources.quote:
latency remains below 5 seconds,i.e.,comparable
to modern payment systems;
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates payment speed on constrained hardware and explores how offline payments can enforce regulatory rules.
sources.not_established: The prototype does not demonstrate its proposed stronger privacy protections or prevent money creation after a protected chip is compromised.

sources.who: Bikash Poudel, Sarah Carey, Robert Flynn and collaborators
sources.showed: A preliminary working paper reports a phone wallet that transfers digital money without internet access. It uses protected chips and mathematical checks to resist counterfeiting and spending the same money twice.
sources.quote:
We implemented the oﬄine protocol in a digital wallet and tested the 
oﬄine token transfer protocol in iOS smartphones using Bluetooth as the transport method.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates offline transfers on consumer smartphones.
sources.not_established: The phone tests do not establish broad deployment, loss recovery or the complete set of privacy and legal safeguards.

sources.who: Foteini Baldimtsi, Melissa Chase, Georg Fuchsbauer and Markulf Kohlweiss
sources.showed: The authors constructed digital coins that can pass between users anonymously before returning to a bank. Their design detects spending the same coin twice without a trusted party able to trace everyone.
sources.quote:
This paper presents the ﬁrst eﬃcient
and fully anonymous transferable e-cash scheme without any trusted
third parties.
sources.cited_for: It supports the mathematical feasibility of anonymous digital money that can change hands repeatedly.
sources.not_established: The construction does not establish a widely usable system with recovery, outage resilience and legally governed access.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated important parts of the capability. Aurum combines privacy with regulatory controls in an exploratory prototype. PayOff adds private offline transfers and identification of counterfeit money flows. Other teams have tested smart-card and phone payments without internet access.
missing: A combined system still needs to preserve valid payments through repeated offline transfers, outages and reconnection at substantial scale.
Recovery must return funds to legitimate owners without enabling duplicate claims or unauthorized access.
Privacy and legally authorized access need independent testing during ordinary payments, device compromise, recovery and investigations.

milestones.label: Legally grounded payments stay valid through offline transfers at scale
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to test repeated offline transfers, outages, reconnection and conflicting payments at substantial scale, with limits set beforehand. This would establish when recipients can safely accept money.

milestones.label: Independent tests establish privacy and limits on exceptional access
milestones.explanation: Independent tests would have to establish what each party can learn during payments, device loss, compromise, recovery and investigations, and test authorization and audits. This would expose access beyond permitted powers.

milestones.label: Repeatable evaluations establish practical limits under realistic conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would need enough design detail to repeat tests of usability, affordability and dependence on devices, power and offline limits. Repeated results would establish how broadly the protections hold.

uncertain: The scale, acceptable failure rates and permitted duration and depth of offline transfers still need clear thresholds.
The acceptable balance between privacy, recovery and investigative powers requires legal and policy choices as well as engineering.
It remains unclear how much privacy can improve without unacceptable costs in speed or operational complexity.

page.title: Privacy-preserving offline central bank digital currency
page.definition: Retail central bank digital currency, money issued by a central bank for public payments, lets disconnected users pay and re-spend receipts without later network approval. It restricts routine disclosure of payment details to payer and payee, enforces payment integrity and legal controls, and recovers interrupted transfers.

goal.need: BIS surveyed 55 central banks representing 71% of the global population. Respondents favoured offline payments and restoration of offline holdings. Offline settlement allows payments during network outages.

figures.caption: BIS central-bank survey, published on 11 May 2023
rows: Restoring offline holdings is vital or advantageous
figures.note: Percentages as reported in Annex B.

statements.quote: When paying offline, only the payer and the payee would know the personal transaction details of the payments made.
statements.context: Digital-euro FAQ updated on 17 August 2026; anti-money-laundering checks apply during funding and defunding.

statements.quote: privacy should be technologically enforced rather than institutionally promised.
statements.context: Project Aurum Phase 2's statement of its design standpoint.

statements.quote: Clear rules would be required for what happens if a device is lost or stolen
statements.context: The exploratory note identifies liability and consumer protection conditions for use at scale; it says a UK case for device offline payments has not been established.

completion.title: A retail CBDC is issued with private offline re-spending and recovery of interrupted transfers.
completion.criterion: A central bank issues a retail CBDC for ordinary use beyond a restricted pilot. Both disconnected users can settle payments and re-spend receipts without routinely disclosing payment details beyond payer and payee; funding and defunding remain subject to legal checks. Under its published secure-device assumptions, the same system rejects replay and redirected payment instructions, enforces the issuer's offline risk limits, and restores interrupted transfers when the wallet connection is immediately restored. Applicable law specifies access to identity and payment data.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis; the cited programmes do not publish a combined acceptance test.
completion.basis: Searched BIS Polaris/Aurum, ECB design and pilot documents, Bank of England offline reports, EU digital-euro proposals and BSI TR-03179. No combined acceptance test or common numerical scale/failure limits was found in accessible documents. The Council's draft Article 23 requires offline availability “as of the first issuance of the digital euro.” This Atlas test uses public issuance and Polaris's interrupted-transfer recovery condition.

milestones.title: A digital-cash prototype validates payments without revealing their private inputs.
milestones.criterion: A prototype validates payments with zero-knowledge proofs, which establish validity without revealing private inputs, and restricts identity and transaction data by actor. Aurum Phase 2 reports this implemented design on 13 October 2026. Its privacy evaluation is a team self-assessment against linking and profiling risks. On an NVIDIA Tesla T4, proof generation took 0.4 seconds for 1 input coin and 1.76 seconds for 20 input coins. These are component timings in an exploratory report, not peer-reviewed deployment results.
milestones.set_by: BIS Innovation Hub, Project Aurum Phase 2, executive summary and Annexes D–E; a prototype objective.
milestones.threshold_quote: allowing transactions to be validated without revealing sensitive payment details.

milestones.title: Offline CBDC recipients can immediately re-spend funds with final and irrevocable settlement.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate final, irrevocable settlement with neither party connected to the CBDC network and receipts immediately re-spendable offline. On 10 April 2025, the Bank of England reported this in all four experimental solutions across smartphones and smart cards; no real money was used. Federal Reserve working paper 2025-105 reports tested iOS/Bluetooth transfers; it is preliminary and not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Bank of England, offline-payment experiment report, project objectives and findings; written for the digital pound.
milestones.threshold_quote: final and irrevocable offline CBDC payments.

milestones.title: Offline CBDC wallets reject replayed payments, duplicate spending and redirection to another wallet.
milestones.criterion: Under Polaris's protected-key and tamper-resistant-device assumptions, wallets reject replay, repeated spending of the same value and redirection to another recipient. The peer-reviewed PayOff paper, published at ASIA CCS in June 2026, reports identifying creators and recipients of counterfeit money after secure-element compromise, providing accountability after hardware breaches.
milestones.set_by: BIS Innovation Hub, Project Polaris handbook, section 5.5.8, Measures to mitigate double-spending risks.
milestones.threshold_quote: Any specific payment instruction should be accepted only once and by only one receiving purse.

milestones.title: Funds are recovered when a synchronous offline CBDC payment fails.
milestones.criterion: A synchronous offline payment flow recovers funds if a payment fails. The recipient acknowledges the transfer. The Bank of England reported this behaviour on 10 April 2025. Its asynchronous flow could lose unclaimed funds; device-loss recovery was outside the experiment.
milestones.set_by: Bank of England, offline-payment experiment report, Synchronous payment flow and Asynchronous payment flow.
milestones.threshold_quote: the synchronous payment flow allowed funds to be recovered if payments failed.

milestones.title: Users settle and re-spend offline CBDC payments in a central-bank operational pilot.
milestones.criterion: Execute the ECB pilot's offline person-to-person use case through near-field communication between disconnected devices, with immediate settlement and re-spending without reconnection. Users are Eurosystem staff; beta money is issued by Eurosystem central banks against funds from payment service providers. The published operational phase lasts 12 months. The FAQ updated on 28 October 2026 describes development, without reporting completed operational payment tests.
milestones.set_by: European Central Bank, digital-euro pilot FAQs Q1, Q3–4, Q8 and Q75; this programme's pilot is for the digital euro.
milestones.threshold_quote: beta digital euro received offline can be re-spent offline without needing to reconnect to the network first.

not_found: No common numerical acceptance limits were found for population, throughput, outage duration, offline transfer depth or failure rates across the combined capability.
No common requirement guaranteeing recovery from a lost or destroyed offline device was found.
No opened source establishes production operation of all completion functions in one CBDC.
The BSI TR-03179-1 guideline and ETH-hosted PayOff full text returned HTTP 403.

results.finding: Aurum Phase 2 developed one exploratory digital-cash proof of concept using zero-knowledge proofs.
results.detail: The page describes privacy-preserving payments and separated data access, but does not state that zero-knowledge proofs validate payments or give proof-generation timings.
results.quote: The project developed an exploratory proof of concept (PoC) that combines encryption, BBS+ signatures, pseudonym-based ownership and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) to support privacy-preserving payments while maintaining mechanisms for compliance.

results.finding: PayOff proposes transferable offline payments with offline settlement; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The source does not report a demonstration of immediate offline re-spending with final, irrevocable settlement.
results.quote: We propose PayOff, an account-based CBDC design for anonymous and transferable offline payments with offline settlement.

results.finding: PayOff identifies creators and recipients of counterfeit money; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The source describes accountability after secure-element compromise but does not report wallets rejecting replay, duplicate spending and redirection.
results.quote: To increase robustness against compromised secure elements and facilitate subsequent prosecution, PayOff ensures that the central bank can identify the creators and recipients of counterfeit money.

results.finding: A two-smart-card prototype supports offline settlement and re-spending.
results.detail: Payment performance was evaluated over five iterations, but the text does not establish final, irrevocable settlement.
results.quote:
value exchangeandtransaction settlement
(i.e.,funds are available for re-spending) occur without the
need for the user(s) to connect to the online ledger.

results.finding: A security analysis reports rejection of replayed payments and prevention of double spending; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The analysis assumes secure elements cannot be compromised. It does not establish rejection of payment redirection to another wallet.
results.quote:
Therefore, intercepted<Receive>messages from previous
transactions cannot be replayed and will be rejected. An
immediate corollary is that an adversary cannot double spend.

results.finding: A retransmission protocol addresses interrupted offline transfers; sample size not stated.
results.detail: The analysis assumes a non-adversarial recipient. The text does not report a failure-recovery experiment or a recipient acknowledgment to the sender.
results.quote:
If the receiving party of a trans-
action is not adversarial, then the retransmission protocol en-
sures that interrupted transactions that result in an incomplete
state can be repeated, ensuring a consistent state between the
two participants and no loss of funds.

results.finding: Prototype offline token transfers were tested between iOS smartphones; the number of transfers is not reported.
results.detail: The model describes instant settlement and offline transfers, but the text does not demonstrate irrevocable settlement and immediate re-spending of receipts. The issuer is unspecified.
results.quote:
We implemented the oﬄine protocol in a digital wallet and tested the 
oﬄine token transfer protocol in iOS smartphones using Bluetooth as the transport method.

results.finding: The prototype uses SignOnce to delete a token ownership key after signing; the number of security tests is not reported.
results.detail: The authors describe double-spending and redirection safeguards under secure-element assumptions, but do not report tests showing rejection of replay, duplicate spending and redirection.
results.quote:
After the successful proof generation, 
the KTOprv is deleted from the key store so that the same token cannot be spent or 
transferred again.

results.finding: One theoretical transferable e-cash construction uses zero-knowledge proofs; no prototype sample size is reported.
results.detail: The paper describes a cryptographic construction and an instantiation, but does not report an implemented prototype or payment-validation measurements.
results.quote: In order to instantiate our scheme we need to make concrete choices for a malleable signature scheme which supports the allowable transformations TCSpend andTCWith, a signature scheme for the signing of certiﬁcates, a randomizable public key encryption scheme, a commitment scheme ( ComSetup, Com) and a zero knowledge proof system ⟨P,V⟩.

results.finding: One theoretical e-cash scheme permits repeated offline coin transfers; no payment-test sample size is reported.
results.detail: The paper does not demonstrate final, irrevocable offline CBDC settlement. Double spending is detected only after both copies are deposited.
results.quote: This paper presents the ﬁrst eﬃcient and fully anonymous transferable e-cash scheme without any trusted third parties.

results.finding: One proposed mechanism identifies a double spender after two copies of a coin are deposited; no test sample size is reported.
results.detail: This is detection after deposit, rather than wallet rejection of replay, duplicate spending and redirection under the specified device assumptions.
results.quote: Note that we cannot detect double-spending unless both of the double-spent coins are deposited.

results.finding: PaxPay’s regulated prototype verified zero-knowledge proofs in 5.6 ms on average across 10 runs.
results.detail: PaxPay implements private payment validation and restricts transaction information by actor. It is a different prototype from the specified Aurum Phase 2 design, and the reported timing is for verification rather than Aurum’s proof-generation measurements.
results.quote:
The results indicate that our SNARK verification time is notably short,
taking only 5.6 ms.

results.finding: All 4 experimental solutions achieved immediate offline settlement and re-spendability.
results.detail: Finality and irrevocability were demonstrated from a technology perspective; legal finality was not assessed. No real money was used.
results.quote: All solutions achieved final and irrevocable payments by transferring funds from the payer to the payee with immediate confirmation and settlement, enabling the payee to spend those funds immediately without having to reconnect to the network.

results.finding: Bank of England experiment: 4 offline payment solutions explored; synchronous flow recovered funds after failed payments.
results.detail: The payee’s device verified and acknowledged the payment. The report does not specify how many solutions used the synchronous flow or how many failed payments were tested. No real money was used; device-loss recovery was outside the experiment.
results.quote: In contrast, the synchronous payment flow allowed funds to be recovered if payments failed.
